client: I got a really bad grade on my final project last week, and I just can't stop thinking about it. It feels like no matter how hard I try, I'm just not smart enough to be in college. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like this grade has really gotten under your skin, and that thought — "I'm just not smart enough" — feels heavy and hard to shake. I'm glad you decided to give this a shot, even with some doubt about whether it'll help, because that kind of honesty is actually a great starting point. Can you tell me a bit more about what "not smart enough" means to you — is this a feeling that showed up just after this grade, or has it been quietly following you around for a while?

client: Honestly, it's not just this grade — that feeling has been around for a long time, like this quiet voice in the back of my head that I've mostly been able to ignore. But when I got that mark back, it was like it got a megaphone all of a sudden. I guess I've always kind of assumed I was just getting by on luck or effort, and that eventually something would prove I wasn't actually capable.
therapist: What you're describing — this sense that you've been "found out" by a bad grade — actually has a name in CBT circles: it's often called impostor thinking, and it's more common than you might imagine, especially among people who care deeply about doing well. It's interesting that you mention luck and effort, almost like you've been giving everything credit *except* your own ability. What would it mean for you if some of your past successes were actually evidence of genuine capability, rather than just luck running in your favor?

client: I mean, I've heard the term "impostor syndrome" before, and part of me gets it intellectually, but it doesn't really make me feel better to know it has a name. Like, okay, lots of people feel this way, but that doesn't change the fact that I got a bad grade and my professor probably sees right through me now. And honestly, the idea that my past successes were "genuine capability" — I want to believe that, but it feels like I'd just be lying to myself, you know?
therapist: That resistance you're feeling makes a lot of sense — knowing something intellectually and *feeling* it are two very different things, and I don't want to just hand you a reframe that doesn't land. What I'm curious about, though, is this idea that believing in your own capability would be "lying to yourself" — because that's a really strong claim, and it's worth examining what evidence you're actually weighing. What would you need to see, or what would have to be true, for it to feel *honest* rather than like self-deception to acknowledge that you might genuinely belong here?

client: That's... actually a harder question than I expected. I think I'd need some kind of proof that isn't just people being polite or obligated to include me, like if someone genuinely sought me out because they wanted my input specifically. But even as I say that, I realize I'd probably find a way to explain it away, like "oh they only asked me because no one else was available" — so maybe the bar I've set for myself is just impossible to clear no matter what happens.
therapist: There's something really insightful happening right now — you just caught yourself in the act of moving the goalposts, and recognizing that pattern is actually a significant moment. It sounds like the "proof" you're asking for isn't really about evidence at all, because your mind has a ready-made explanation to dismiss whatever shows up. What do you think it would feel like to just sit with the possibility that this system your mind has built — where nothing can ever count as proof — might be protecting you from something rather than telling you the truth?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually gets it — like, intellectually I can see that I keep shifting what would count as proof that I'm not a burden to the people in my life. But sitting with that idea that my mind might be "protecting" me feels almost insulting, like you're saying I'm making this up or that my loneliness isn't real. Because it feels very real to me, even if I can't fully explain why no one ever seems to reach out first.
therapist: Your loneliness is absolutely real, and I want to be clear that I'm not suggesting you're making anything up — that wasn't my intention at all, and I'm glad you pushed back on that. What I was trying to point to isn't that the pain is invented, but that the *story* your mind tells about *why* you're lonely — that you're a burden, that people don't genuinely want you around — might be worth separating from the loneliness itself. When you notice that no one reaches out first, what's the very first thought that comes to you about what that means?

client: When no one reaches out first, the very first thing that hits me is just... "See, I knew it." Like it confirms something I already suspected about myself, that I'm just not someone people think about when they're going about their day. It's not even a dramatic thought, it's more like a quiet, heavy kind of knowing that settles in my chest.
therapist: That quiet, heavy "see, I knew it" is actually one of the most important things you've shared — it's not a loud, panicked thought, it's something that feels like settled truth, which makes it especially hard to question. In CBT we'd call that a "confirmation bias" at work, where your mind is primed to notice every silence as proof, while moments where people *do* show up get quietly filed away as exceptions. I'm wondering — when you think back over the past few months, are there any moments, even small ones, where someone *did* seek you out or show they were thinking of you, that you might have explained away at the time?

client: I mean... yeah, my coworker did text me last month just to check in, not about work or anything, just to ask how I was doing. But honestly my first thought was that she probably sent that to a bunch of people, like it was some kind of group check-in thing she does. I didn't really let myself take it in as meaning anything specific to me.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you remembered that moment, and I notice you held it at arm's length almost immediately — your mind went straight to finding a reason it didn't count, before you even let yourself feel it. That's that same pattern we were talking about, the moving goalposts, but now we can see it happening with a real, specific moment. What do you think it would have felt like in your body if you had allowed yourself, just for a second, to take that text in as genuine — that she was thinking specifically about *you*?

client: I mean... if I really try to imagine that, I think it would have felt kind of warm, maybe in my chest? But honestly even trying to picture it right now makes me want to pull back, like there's this reflex that kicks in and says "don't get comfortable with this, you'll just be disappointed." It's easier to just not let it land than to feel it and then have it taken away somehow.
therapist: That warmth you described, even just imagining it, tells you something important — part of you *wants* to let connection in, and that part is still there even after years of protecting yourself from disappointment. The reflex to pull back makes complete sense as a survival strategy, like your heart learned early on that hoping can hurt, so it's safer to stay one step removed. I'm curious — do you have a sense of when that reflex first showed up for you, or does it feel like it's just always been there?

client: I think it showed up pretty early, honestly. I remember being maybe nine or ten and my parents would make plans with me and then cancel last minute, or just forget entirely, and after a while I stopped getting excited about things because the letdown felt worse than never hoping at all. So yeah, I guess it's been a long time, which is kind of why I wonder if it's even possible to unlearn something that's been baked in for that long.
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage — that nine-year-old learned something very logical given what was happening: *don't hope, and you won't hurt*. It makes complete sense that it's felt "baked in," because it was learned at a time when you had no other choice. But here's something worth holding onto — the fact that you could feel that warmth in your chest just imagining your coworker's text, even briefly, suggests that the capacity for connection hasn't been erased, just carefully guarded. What do you think that younger version of you would have needed to hear back then that maybe you've never quite let yourself believe?

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because I don't think anyone's ever asked me that before. I guess... that younger me needed to hear that it was okay to want people, that needing someone didn't automatically mean getting hurt or abandoned. But even saying that out loud feels almost embarrassing, like I'm admitting to something I'm not supposed to want.
therapist: There's nothing embarrassing about what you just said — wanting connection is one of the most fundamentally human things there is, and the fact that it feels like a shameful secret says a lot about what you had to learn to survive, not about what you're actually allowed to want. That younger you wasn't asking for too much; he was asking for exactly what every child deserves. I wonder if, gently and slowly, part of our work together could be about giving yourself permission to want that now — not as something to be earned or proven worthy of, but just as something that's okay to need. What feels most scary about allowing yourself to want that?
